t: Linked List Components — Counting Maximal Runs with a Hash Set
o: We must count maximal runs of consecutive linked-list nodes whose values all appear in `nums`. A new component starts whenever the current node is in `nums` and the previous node was not (or we are at the head). In Example 1, `[0,1]` is one run (0→1 both in nums), node 2 breaks it, and `[3]` is a second run. In Example 2, runs are `[0,1]` and `[3,4]`. Since values are unique and bounded by n, a hash set gives O(1) membership checks; a single pass over the list suffices.
k: A component boundary occurs exactly when a node is in nums but its predecessor is not (or it is the head).
Storing nums in a hash set turns each membership test into O(1), enabling a single linear scan.
You never need to modify the list or track component contents — only count run starts.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Linear Search
a.i: For every node in the list, check whether its value is in `nums` by scanning the array. Count a new component when the current node is in `nums` while the previous node was not. This works but costs O(n·m) time for m = len(nums), which can be 10^8 operations at worst — borderline but instructive as a baseline.
s: For each node, linearly scan nums to test membership of node.val.
If current is in nums and prevIn is false, increment count.
Set prevIn to the current membership result and advance the node.
a.t: O(n · m) where n is list length and m = nums.length — each node triggers a linear scan of nums.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input.

a.i: Put all values of `nums` into a hash set so membership checks are O(1). Then walk the list once, counting a component start whenever the current value is in the set and the previous value was not (or there is no previous node). This correctly counts maximal runs because every run has exactly one such 'start' node.
s: Traverse the list; compute curIn = set.contains(cur.val).
If curIn and not prevIn, increment count.
Update prevIn = curIn and advance; return count.

c.python:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def numComponents(self, head: Optional[ListNode], nums: List[int]) -> int:
        s = set(nums)
        count, prevIn = 0, False
        cur = head
        while cur:
            curIn = cur.val in s
            if curIn and not prevIn:
                count += 1
            prevIn = curIn
            cur = cur.next
        return count

a.t: O(n + m) — building the set is O(m) and the single traversal does O(1) work per node.

a.i: Since every value satisfies 0 <= Node.val < n, replace the hash set with a fixed-size boolean array indexed by value. This removes hashing overhead and guarantees O(1) lookups with no collisions, often faster in practice in C++/Java.
s: Let n be determined by walking the list once (or use max value + 1); allocate a boolean array of that size.
Mark present[v] = true for each v in nums.
Traverse the list counting run starts as before using array lookups.

c.python:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def numComponents(self, head: Optional[ListNode], nums: List[int]) -> int:
        n, cur = 0, head
        while cur:
            n += 1
            cur = cur.next
        present = [False] * n
        for v in nums:
            present[v] = True
        count, prevIn = 0, False
        cur = head
        while cur:
            curIn = present[cur.val]
            if curIn and not prevIn:
                count += 1
            prevIn = curIn
            cur = cur.next
        return count

a.t: O(n + m) — two passes over the list plus one pass over nums, all with O(1) array operations.

w: In an interview, lead with the hash-set single pass (Approach 2): it is simple, optimal asymptotically, and easy to explain. Mention Approach 3 as a micro-optimization when values are small non-negative integers, and skip the brute force unless asked to warm up. Common pitfalls: forgetting that the head itself can start a component (initialize prevIn = false handles this), double-counting by incrementing on every in-nums node instead of only run starts, and assuming nums order matters (it does not). Edge cases: entire list in nums (answer 1), disjoint single nodes (answer = number of matches), and a single-node list. Follow-ups might ask for O(1) extra space (impossible without destroying the set requirement unless you sort nums and binary search, giving O((n+m) log m) time and O(1)/O(sort) space), or handling duplicate values in the list.
